Chapter 6: The Practice of Forgiveness—Healing Old Wounds.
Forgiveness isn’t usually some big, dramatic moment. More often, it’s this slow, sometimes painful process that unfolds quietly in the heart. You know how most of us carry around old hurts, almost like invisible stones in our pockets? They weigh us down, even if we barely notice.
What if you could look at those burdens with gentle honesty? Because the truth is, the past shapes so much of our present. And forgiveness? It can set you free in ways you might not expect.
Let me share a story. There was someone who, for years, avoided family gatherings because of a falling out with their sibling. Every get-together felt like walking through a minefield, with resentment hanging in the air. But after spending yet another lonely holiday alone, they realized something: they wanted connection more than they feared being hurt again.
Sitting quietly, they remembered an important truth. Forgiveness isn’t about excusing what happened. It’s about letting go of pain’s tight grip.
The first step? Just acknowledging the hurt—without judgment. Not easy, right? All those old memories rise up—angry words, moments of betrayal. But as they allowed themselves to really feel that pain, something inside started to soften.
They saw how holding onto resentment was like drinking poison, hoping the other person would get sick. Most people don’t even realize how much energy it takes to keep old wounds alive.
Bit by bit, they began to see their sibling differently—not as an enemy, but as another human being. Flawed, struggling, and deserving of compassion. The journey wasn’t a straight line. Some days, the anger came back. Other days, there was a surprising sense of peace. Over time, the urge to be right just faded, replaced by a quiet willingness to let go.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: forgiveness is a gift we give ourselves. It doesn’t mean forgetting, or saying what happened was okay. It means choosing freedom over bitterness, love over fear. So many of us replay old stories, thinking that holding on will keep us safe from getting hurt again. But real safety? It comes from opening your heart, not closing it off.
Forgiveness, just like love, is a practice. It’s something you return to, over and over, whenever those old wounds start to resurface.
And sometimes, the hardest person to forgive is yourself. There’s a story in the book about someone haunted by regret—convinced they weren’t worthy of happiness because of past mistakes. But the moment they started treating themselves with the same compassion they offered to others, that heavy burden finally began to lift.
So, if you’re carrying something heavy, remember—healing begins with a single step. And every time you choose forgiveness, you’re choosing freedom.
